stem: Which pre-endoscopy score identifies patients with upper GI bleeding at very low risk who may be managed as outpatients?
explanation: ESGE and ACG recommend the Glasgow–Blatchford score for pre-endoscopy risk stratification; patients scoring 0–1 have very low risk of needing intervention or dying and can be managed as outpatients. The full Rockall score requires endoscopic findings.
referenceText: Gralnek et al. 2021 (ESGE non-variceal UGIB) [80]; Laine et al. 2021 (ACG upper GI bleeding) [122]

stem: In a patient with acute upper GI bleeding without cardiovascular disease, what haemoglobin threshold for red cell transfusion is recommended?
explanation: Villanueva et al. showed a restrictive strategy (threshold 7 g/dL) reduced mortality and rebleeding compared with a liberal strategy (9 g/dL), especially in cirrhosis. ESGE recommends a threshold of 7 g/dL (target 7–9) without cardiovascular disease, and a higher threshold of 8 g/dL with cardiovascular disease.
referenceText: Villanueva et al. 2013 (transfusion in UGIB) [226]; Gralnek et al. 2021 (ESGE non-variceal UGIB) [80]

stem: A haemodynamically resuscitated patient has suspected non-variceal upper GI bleeding with Glasgow–Blatchford score of 12. When should endoscopy be performed according to ESGE 2021?

options.A: Within 24 hours of presentation, after haemodynamic resuscitation
options.B: Within 2 hours in all patients regardless of stability

explanation: ESGE recommends early endoscopy (within 24 hours) after resuscitation for non-variceal upper GI bleeding. Urgent endoscopy within 12 hours did not reduce mortality in high-risk patients in a randomised trial. Haemodynamic instability persisting despite resuscitation may require earlier intervention.
referenceText: Gralnek et al. 2021 (ESGE non-variceal UGIB) [80]

stem: At endoscopy, a duodenal ulcer shows a non-bleeding visible vessel. What is its Forrest class, and what treatment is recommended?

options.A: Forrest IIa; endoscopic haemostasis followed by high-dose PPI
options.B: Forrest Ia; surgery without any endoscopic attempt first

explanation: Forrest Ia (spurting) and Ib (oozing) are active bleeding; IIa is a non-bleeding visible vessel; IIb an adherent clot; IIc a flat pigmented spot; III a clean base. Endoscopic haemostasis is recommended for Ia, Ib and IIa lesions, followed by high-dose PPI for 72 hours.
referenceText: Gralnek et al. 2021 (ESGE non-variceal UGIB) [80]

stem: After successful endoscopic haemostasis for a bleeding peptic ulcer with high-risk stigmata, which PPI regimen is recommended?

options.A: High-dose PPI (bolus, then continuous or intermittent) for 72 hours, then oral twice daily
options.D: No PPI is needed, because endoscopic therapy alone is sufficient after haemostasis is achieved

explanation: High-dose PPI therapy for 72 hours after endoscopic haemostasis reduces rebleeding, surgery and mortality. Intermittent high-dose bolus dosing is non-inferior to continuous infusion. Twice-daily oral PPI is continued for up to 14 days, then once daily depending on ulcer aetiology.
referenceText: Gralnek et al. 2021 (ESGE non-variceal UGIB) [80]; Laine et al. 2021 (ACG upper GI bleeding) [122]

stem: A patient rebleeds 24 hours after endoscopic therapy for a gastric ulcer. What is the recommended next step?

options.C: Repeat endoscopic haemostasis; if it fails, arterial embolisation or surgery
options.D: Tranexamic acid infusion as definitive therapy, avoiding repeat endoscopy

explanation: ESGE recommends a second endoscopic attempt for rebleeding; if this fails, transcatheter angiographic embolisation (TAE) is preferred, with surgery when TAE is unavailable or unsuccessful. Over-the-scope clips are an option for recurrent bleeding.
referenceText: Gralnek et al. 2021 (ESGE non-variceal UGIB) [80]; Laine et al. 2021 (ACG upper GI bleeding) [122]

stem: What did the HALT-IT trial show for high-dose IV tranexamic acid in acute GI bleeding?

options.C: No fewer bleeding deaths, but more venous thromboembolism and seizures
options.E: Reduced rebleeding in variceal bleeding only, with no effect on mortality

explanation: HALT-IT randomised 12,009 patients and found no reduction in death due to bleeding, while venous thromboembolic events and seizures were more frequent. Routine high-dose tranexamic acid is not recommended for GI bleeding.
referenceText: HALT-IT Collaborators 2020 [85]

stem: A patient with cirrhosis presents with haematemesis and suspected variceal bleeding. Besides resuscitation, which combination should be started before endoscopy?

options.A: Platelet transfusion to above 100 × 10⁹/L and FFP to correct the INR before urgent endoscopy
options.B: Vitamin K and FFP to normalise INR
options.C: A vasoactive drug (terlipressin, somatostatin or octreotide) plus antibiotic prophylaxis

explanation: Baveno VII recommends starting vasoactive drugs as soon as variceal bleeding is suspected (continued 2–5 days), antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone 1 g/24 h up to 7 days) and endoscopy within 12 hours. Correcting INR with FFP is not recommended, as INR does not reflect bleeding risk in cirrhosis.
referenceText: de Franchis et al. 2022 (Baveno VII) [47]; EASL 2018 (decompensated cirrhosis) [64]

stem: A patient with Child–Pugh C cirrhosis (score 11) has oesophageal variceal bleeding controlled by vasoactive drugs and band ligation. What does Baveno VII recommend?

options.D: Pre-emptive TIPS within 72 hours (ideally within 24 hours)

explanation: Pre-emptive TIPS reduces rebleeding and mortality in high-risk patients: Child–Pugh C (score below 14) or Child–Pugh B above 7 with active bleeding at endoscopy, or HVPG above 20 mmHg. It should be placed within 72 hours, ideally 24 hours.
referenceText: de Franchis et al. 2022 (Baveno VII) [47]

stem: Despite vasoactive drugs and band ligation, a patient continues to bleed massively from oesophageal varices. What is the most appropriate bridging therapy before rescue TIPS?

options.A: Balloon tamponade or a self-expanding oesophageal metal stent
options.C: Increase terlipressin to a 10 mg bolus and repeat band ligation within 6 hours

explanation: Refractory variceal bleeding can be temporarily controlled by balloon tamponade (for up to 24 hours) or self-expanding metal stents (which have fewer complications) as a bridge to rescue TIPS. Airway protection is usually required before balloon placement.
referenceText: de Franchis et al. 2022 (Baveno VII) [47]; EASL 2018 (decompensated cirrhosis) [64]

stem: Which is the first-line endoscopic treatment for bleeding isolated fundal (IGV1) or gastro-oesophageal type 2 gastric varices?
explanation: Cyanoacrylate injection is preferred for bleeding fundal varices (GOV2 and IGV1), with TIPS or balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration (BRTO) as alternatives. GOV1 varices extending along the lesser curve can be treated like oesophageal varices.
referenceText: de Franchis et al. 2022 (Baveno VII) [47]

stem: An Egyptian farmer with chronic Schistosoma mansoni infection presents with variceal bleeding. Liver function tests and synthetic function are normal, and ultrasound shows periportal ("pipestem") fibrosis. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Hepatic encephalopathy is the most common presentation
options.B: The condition responds to corticosteroids alone
options.C: Presinusoidal portal hypertension; manage bleeding as in cirrhosis and treat with praziquantel
options.D: Liver transplantation is the first-line treatment
options.E: The hepatic venous pressure gradient is markedly elevated in all cases, exactly as in cirrhosis

explanation: Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis causes periportal (Symmers') fibrosis and presinusoidal portal hypertension with splenomegaly and varices, but hepatocellular function is usually preserved unless coexisting viral hepatitis (common in Egypt) is present. HVPG may be normal. Acute bleeding is managed with vasoactive drugs and endoscopic therapy.
referenceText: de Franchis et al. 2022 (Baveno VII) [47]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A patient with severe haematochezia remains haemodynamically unstable despite resuscitation; an upper source has been excluded. What does the ACG 2023 guideline suggest as the next diagnostic step?

options.B: Elective colonoscopy after bowel preparation in 72 hours
options.E: CT angiography to localise bleeding before transcatheter embolisation

explanation: In haemodynamically unstable lower GI bleeding, CT angiography localises active bleeding and guides catheter angiography with embolisation. Upper GI bleeding should be excluded, as up to 15% of severe haematochezia arises from an upper source.
referenceText: Sengupta et al. 2023 (ACG lower GI bleeding) [193]

stem: A patient with acute pancreatitis develops respiratory failure that persists for 72 hours. According to the revised Atlanta classification, how is the severity classified?

options.D: Interstitial oedematous pancreatitis without severity grading

explanation: Revised Atlanta: mild (no organ failure or local complications), moderately severe (transient organ failure under 48 hours and/or local or systemic complications) and severe (persistent organ failure beyond 48 hours). Persistent organ failure is the main determinant of mortality.
referenceText: Banks et al. 2013 (revised Atlanta classification) [14]

stem: What did the WATERFALL trial show regarding fluid resuscitation in acute pancreatitis?

options.A: Saline was superior to lactated Ringer's
options.B: Fluid volume did not affect fluid overload
options.C: Aggressive resuscitation reduced progression to moderately severe or severe disease and mortality
options.E: Aggressive resuscitation caused more fluid overload without better outcomes than moderate

explanation: WATERFALL was stopped early because aggressive fluid (20 mL/kg bolus then 3 mL/kg/h) increased fluid overload (20.5% vs 6.3%) without reducing moderately severe or severe pancreatitis. Goal-directed moderate resuscitation with lactated Ringer's solution is now favoured.
referenceText: de-Madaria et al. 2022 (WATERFALL) [48]; IAP/APA 2013 (acute pancreatitis guideline) [239]

stem: Which statement about antibiotics in severe acute pancreatitis is correct?

options.B: Antibiotics should be given to all patients with CRP above 150 mg/L
options.C: Prophylactic carbapenems for 14 days are recommended in all patients with necrotising pancreatitis
options.D: Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended; treat only proven or suspected infection

explanation: IAP/APA and other guidelines recommend against prophylactic antibiotics in acute pancreatitis regardless of severity. Infected necrosis is suspected with clinical deterioration or gas on CT, and antibiotics penetrating necrosis (e.g. carbapenems) are used together with delayed drainage.
referenceText: IAP/APA 2013 (acute pancreatitis guideline) [239]

stem: A patient with necrotising pancreatitis develops suspected infected necrosis at 3 weeks. Which strategy is recommended?

options.C: Antibiotics and delayed step-up drainage (percutaneous or endoscopic) once walled-off
options.D: Antibiotics alone for 6 months without any drainage, necrosectomy or other intervention

explanation: The PANTER trial showed that a step-up approach (percutaneous drainage followed, if needed, by minimally invasive necrosectomy) reduced major complications and death compared with primary open necrosectomy. Intervention is delayed until encapsulation (walled-off necrosis), around 4 weeks.
referenceText: van Santvoort et al. 2010 (PANTER) [224]; IAP/APA 2013 (acute pancreatitis guideline) [239]

stem: How should nutrition be provided in predicted severe acute pancreatitis?

options.A: Oral fat-free diet only after 10 days
options.C: Enteral feeding only after normalisation of serum lipase and resolution of abdominal pain
options.D: Early enteral nutrition (nasogastric or nasojejunal) rather than parenteral

explanation: Enteral nutrition maintains gut barrier function and reduces infectious complications and mortality compared with parenteral nutrition. Nasogastric feeding is as safe as nasojejunal in most patients. Parenteral nutrition is reserved for enteral intolerance.
referenceText: IAP/APA 2013 (acute pancreatitis guideline) [239]; Singer et al. 2019 (ESPEN ICU nutrition) [199]

stem: When is urgent ERCP (within 24 hours) indicated in gallstone pancreatitis?

options.B: When the patient has mild pancreatitis
options.C: In all patients with gallstone pancreatitis
options.E: When there is concomitant acute cholangitis

explanation: Urgent ERCP is indicated in gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis. ERCP is probably indicated for persistent biliary obstruction, but routine urgent ERCP in predicted severe gallstone pancreatitis without cholangitis did not improve outcomes (APEC trial). Cholecystectomy prevents recurrence.
referenceText: IAP/APA 2013 (acute pancreatitis guideline) [239]

stem: A patient with pancreatitis has triglycerides of 3200 mg/dL (36 mmol/L). Which therapy is used to lower triglycerides rapidly?

options.C: An oral fibrate as the sole acute treatment, together with strict dietary fat restriction
options.E: Insulin infusion (with glucose if needed); consider plasmapheresis in selected cases

explanation: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia (above about 1000 mg/dL or 11.3 mmol/L) causes pancreatitis. Insulin activates lipoprotein lipase, rapidly lowering triglycerides; plasmapheresis can be used in severe cases. Lipid-containing infusions such as propofol should be minimised.
referenceText: IAP/APA 2013 (acute pancreatitis guideline) [239]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: Which definition best describes acute liver failure?

options.A: INR ≥1.5 and encephalopathy without pre-existing cirrhosis, with illness under 26 weeks
options.C: Encephalopathy in a patient with long-standing cirrhosis
options.D: Hepatitis B reactivation with normal INR
options.E: Bilirubin above 50 µmol/L with ascites and encephalopathy in a patient with known cirrhosis

explanation: ALF is defined by severe acute liver injury with coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) and hepatic encephalopathy in a patient without prior liver disease, within 26 weeks. It is subclassified as hyperacute (under 7 days), acute (8–28 days) and subacute (4–12 weeks), which influences cerebral oedema risk and prognosis.
referenceText: Wendon et al. 2017 (EASL acute liver failure) [234]

stem: According to the King's College criteria, which finding indicates the need for liver transplantation listing in paracetamol-induced ALF?

options.A: Arterial pH below 7.30 after adequate fluid resuscitation
options.B: Serum paracetamol level above the treatment line

explanation: King's College criteria for paracetamol ALF: arterial pH below 7.30 after resuscitation, or all of INR above 6.5, creatinine above 300 µmol/L and grade 3–4 encephalopathy within 24 hours. Elevated lactate after resuscitation was added in modified criteria. ALT levels do not predict outcome.
referenceText: Wendon et al. 2017 (EASL acute liver failure) [234]; Chiew et al. 2020 (paracetamol poisoning guideline) [36]

stem: A patient with hyperacute ALF has arterial ammonia of 220 µmol/L and grade 4 encephalopathy. Which measure reduces the risk of intracranial hypertension?

options.C: Keep serum sodium 145–155 mmol/L with hypertonic saline; consider CRRT for ammonia
options.D: Lactulose via nasogastric tube as the main therapy to lower ammonia and prevent oedema

explanation: Arterial ammonia above 150–200 µmol/L predicts cerebral oedema in ALF. EASL recommends inducing hypernatraemia (145–155 mmol/L), early CRRT to reduce ammonia, sedation, avoiding hyperthermia and short-term hyperventilation only for surges. Lactulose has no proven benefit in ALF and may cause distension.
referenceText: Wendon et al. 2017 (EASL acute liver failure) [234]

stem: A patient with ALF has INR 4.5 without bleeding. No procedure is planned. What is the recommended approach?

options.A: Avoid routine INR correction; it is prognostic and haemostasis is often rebalanced
options.B: Transfuse platelets to above 150 × 10⁹/L and give FFP to normalise the INR pre-emptively

explanation: In ALF, decreases in procoagulant factors are balanced by reductions in natural anticoagulants; viscoelastic tests are often normal. Prophylactic correction of INR is not recommended, as it obscures prognostic information and adds volume. Vitamin K should be given once.
referenceText: Wendon et al. 2017 (EASL acute liver failure) [234]

stem: A patient with cirrhosis has grade 3 hepatic encephalopathy. A precipitant has been treated. Which therapy is first line?

options.D: Protein restriction to 20 g/day until the encephalopathy has completely resolved
options.E: Lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools daily, adding rifaximin for recurrence

explanation: Lactulose is the first-line treatment of overt hepatic encephalopathy; rifaximin is added to prevent recurrence. Protein restriction is not recommended (1.2–1.5 g/kg/day protein). Precipitants such as GI bleeding, infection, electrolyte disturbance, constipation and sedatives must be identified and treated.
referenceText: Vilstrup et al. 2014 (AASLD/EASL hepatic encephalopathy) [228]

stem: A patient with cirrhosis and ascites has ascitic fluid neutrophils of 420 cells/mm³ and creatinine 150 µmol/L. Besides antibiotics, what therapy reduces renal failure and mortality?

options.C: Terlipressin for 14 days in all patients
options.D: IV albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3

explanation: SBP is diagnosed by ascitic neutrophils of 250 cells/mm³ or more. EASL recommends empirical antibiotics (e.g. third-generation cephalosporin, adjusted for nosocomial risk) and IV albumin (1.5 g/kg at diagnosis and 1 g/kg on day 3), which reduces renal failure and mortality, particularly with renal dysfunction or jaundice.
referenceText: EASL 2018 (decompensated cirrhosis) [64]

stem: Which criterion is required to diagnose hepatorenal syndrome–AKI?

options.D: No response after 2 days of diuretic withdrawal and albumin 1 g/kg
options.E: Microhaematuria above 50 red cells per high-power field on urine microscopy

explanation: ICA criteria for HRS-AKI include cirrhosis with ascites, AKI by ICA-KDIGO criteria, no response after 2 days of diuretic withdrawal and albumin (1 g/kg), and absence of shock, nephrotoxic drugs and structural kidney injury (proteinuria above 500 mg/day, microhaematuria, abnormal ultrasound).
referenceText: Angeli et al. 2015 (ICA AKI in cirrhosis) [8]; EASL 2018 (decompensated cirrhosis) [64]

stem: What did the CONFIRM trial show for terlipressin plus albumin in hepatorenal syndrome type 1?

options.B: Reduced 90-day mortality with no adverse effects compared with placebo plus albumin
options.E: More HRS reversal, but more respiratory failure, especially with volume overload

explanation: CONFIRM showed verified HRS reversal in 32% with terlipressin vs 17% with placebo, but serious respiratory failure was more common (14% vs 5%), related to fluid overload and severe ACLF. Careful volume assessment and avoidance in patients with hypoxaemia are recommended.
referenceText: Wong et al. 2021 (CONFIRM, terlipressin) [237]; EASL 2018 (decompensated cirrhosis) [64]

stem: A patient with tense ascites undergoes paracentesis of 8 L. What is recommended to prevent paracentesis-induced circulatory dysfunction?

options.A: Albumin only if more than 15 L are removed
options.D: IV albumin 8 g per litre of ascites removed

explanation: When more than 5 L of ascites are removed, EASL recommends albumin 8 g/L removed (about 64 g for 8 L) to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction, which causes hyponatraemia, renal impairment and increased mortality.
referenceText: EASL 2018 (decompensated cirrhosis) [64]

stem: Which description best characterises acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) as defined by the EASL-CLIF consortium?

options.A: Liver failure in a patient without prior liver disease, with an illness lasting under 26 weeks
options.B: Acute decompensation of cirrhosis with organ failure and high short-term mortality

explanation: The CANONIC study defined ACLF as acute decompensation of cirrhosis with organ failure (liver, kidney, brain, coagulation, circulation, respiration) and 28-day mortality above 15%. Mortality rises with ACLF grade; grade 3 has 28-day mortality around 75% and may warrant consideration of transplantation.
referenceText: Moreau et al. 2013 (CANONIC, ACLF) [142]; EASL 2018 (decompensated cirrhosis) [64]

stem: A patient with severe alcohol-associated hepatitis (Maddrey discriminant function 45) is started on prednisolone 40 mg/day. On day 7, the Lille score is 0.62. What is the appropriate action?

options.B: Add pentoxifylline and continue both drugs for 3 months
options.C: Stop corticosteroids: the patient is a non-responder
options.D: Increase the prednisolone dose to 80 mg/day

explanation: Patients with Maddrey ≥32 may receive prednisolone. A Lille score above 0.45 at day 7 indicates non-response and poor survival; steroids should be stopped. STOPAH showed a non-significant short-term mortality reduction with prednisolone and no benefit of pentoxifylline.
referenceText: Thursz et al. 2015 (STOPAH) [212]; EASL 2018 (decompensated cirrhosis) [64]

stem: An elderly patient with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden severe abdominal pain out of proportion to examination findings. Lactate is mildly raised. What is the recommended diagnostic test?

options.D: Wait for lactate to exceed 4 mmol/L before imaging

explanation: ESVS recommends CT angiography as first-line imaging for suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia. Embolic occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery is classic in AF. Lactate is non-specific and may be normal early; delays increase bowel necrosis and mortality.
referenceText: Björck et al. 2017 (ESVS mesenteric disease) [19]

stem: How should intra-abdominal pressure be measured according to WSACS guidelines?

options.A: At end-inspiration with the head elevated 45°
options.B: Via a nasogastric tube in the sitting position
options.C: Via the bladder after instilling 200 mL of saline, with the patient sitting upright at 30°
options.D: Via the bladder with ≤25 mL saline, supine, at end-expiration, zeroed at midaxillary line

explanation: WSACS standardises IAP measurement as intravesical pressure (maximum 25 mL instillation), expressed in mmHg, at end-expiration, supine, with absent abdominal muscle contractions and the transducer zeroed at the iliac crest in the midaxillary line.
referenceText: Kirkpatrick et al. 2013 (WSACS abdominal compartment syndrome) [114]

stem: How is abdominal compartment syndrome defined by WSACS?

options.B: Intra-abdominal pressure above 10 mmHg with ileus and abdominal distension
options.E: Sustained IAP above 20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction or failure

explanation: IAH is sustained IAP of 12 mmHg or more, graded I (12–15), II (16–20), III (21–25) and IV (above 25 mmHg). ACS is sustained IAP above 20 mmHg (with or without abdominal perfusion pressure below 60 mmHg) associated with new organ dysfunction. Decompressive laparotomy is used for overt ACS.
referenceText: Kirkpatrick et al. 2013 (WSACS abdominal compartment syndrome) [114]

stem: A critically ill patient after major burns develops fever, right upper quadrant tenderness and a distended, thick-walled gallbladder with pericholecystic fluid but no stones. He is too unstable for surgery. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Acute acalculous cholecystitis occurs in critically ill patients (burns, trauma, sepsis, prolonged fasting, TPN) due to stasis and ischaemia. It progresses quickly to gangrene and perforation. Percutaneous cholecystostomy is the preferred source control in unstable patients.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A ventilated patient develops massive colonic distension without mechanical obstruction; caecal diameter is 12 cm despite 48 hours of conservative management. What is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment?

options.A: Neostigmine 2 mg IV slowly, with cardiac monitoring and atropine ready
options.E: Erythromycin infusion as definitive therapy, with rectal tube placement

explanation: Neostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, produced rapid decompression in most patients in a randomised trial. Bradycardia is the main risk, requiring monitoring and atropine. Contraindications include mechanical obstruction and perforation; colonoscopic decompression is used if it fails.
referenceText: Ponec et al. 1999 (neostigmine for colonic pseudo-obstruction) [167]

stem: What did the REVISE trial show regarding pantoprazole in invasively ventilated patients?

options.C: Less clinically important upper GI bleeding, without differences in mortality or pneumonia
options.E: Significantly increased C. difficile infection and ventilator-associated pneumonia rates overall

explanation: REVISE randomised 4821 ventilated patients; pantoprazole reduced clinically important upper GI bleeding (1.0% vs 3.5%) without significant differences in 90-day mortality, ventilator-associated pneumonia or C. difficile infection. A possible mortality signal in the most severely ill patients was noted.
referenceText: Cook et al. 2024 (REVISE) [39]; Krag et al. 2018 (SUP-ICU) [119]

stem: A ventilated patient on enteral feeding has gastric residual volume above 500 mL on two occasions. What does ESPEN recommend?

options.A: Delay feeding and consider IV erythromycin; post-pyloric feeding if intolerance persists
options.D: Stop enteral feeding permanently and start full parenteral nutrition immediately instead

explanation: ESPEN suggests delaying enteral nutrition when gastric residual volume exceeds 500 mL/6 h and recommends IV erythromycin as first-line prokinetic, with metoclopramide as an alternative. Post-pyloric feeding is suggested when prokinetics fail; ASPEN discourages routine GRV monitoring.
referenceText: Singer et al. 2019 (ESPEN ICU nutrition) [199]; Compher et al. 2022 (ASPEN critical care nutrition) [38]

stem: A patient resuscitated from cardiogenic shock has ALT 4200 U/L and LDH markedly raised on day 2, falling by 50% within 72 hours. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.C: Acute Budd–Chiari syndrome with hepatic vein thrombosis

explanation: Hypoxic hepatitis follows hypoperfusion or hypoxaemia, causing massive transaminase rises (often above 1000 U/L) with high LDH, typically peaking within 24–48 hours and falling rapidly with haemodynamic recovery. It is associated with high mortality reflecting the underlying illness.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Wendon et al. 2017 (EASL acute liver failure) [234]

stem: A patient with cirrhosis has dyspnoea and hypoxaemia that worsens when upright (orthodeoxia). Contrast echocardiography shows bubbles in the left atrium after 4 cardiac cycles. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Hepatopulmonary syndrome results from intrapulmonary vascular dilatations causing V/Q mismatch and shunt, worse in the upright position (orthodeoxia, platypnoea). Delayed appearance of bubbles (after 3–6 cycles) indicates intrapulmonary shunting; liver transplantation is curative.
referenceText: EASL 2018 (decompensated cirrhosis) [64]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: Which feature distinguishes portopulmonary hypertension from hepatopulmonary syndrome?

options.B: Intrapulmonary vasodilatation with delayed bubble passage on contrast echocardiography
options.E: Raised pulmonary vascular resistance with PAH on right heart catheterisation

explanation: Portopulmonary hypertension is pulmonary arterial hypertension in the setting of portal hypertension, caused by vasoconstriction and remodelling. Moderate–severe disease markedly increases liver transplant risk and requires pulmonary vasodilator therapy.
referenceText: EASL 2018 (decompensated cirrhosis) [64]

stem: Which sedative strategy is preferred in a ventilated patient with decompensated cirrhosis?

options.B: Short-acting propofol or dexmedetomidine, avoiding benzodiazepines
options.C: Continuous midazolam infusion, with a daily sedation interruption and lactulose

explanation: Benzodiazepines accumulate in liver failure, precipitate hepatic encephalopathy and prolong ventilation. Short-acting drugs such as propofol, dexmedetomidine and remifentanil are preferred, with dose adjustment and daily interruption.
referenceText: Vilstrup et al. 2014 (AASLD/EASL hepatic encephalopathy) [228]; Devlin et al. 2018 (SCCM PADIS guideline) [54]

stem: Before a central line insertion in a patient with cirrhosis and INR 2.1, which statement is correct?

options.A: FFP must be given to normalise the INR before any invasive procedure, including line insertion
options.B: Central lines are contraindicated in cirrhosis
options.C: Vitamin K reliably corrects the INR in cirrhosis
options.D: INR poorly predicts bleeding; avoid prophylactic plasma and use ultrasound guidance
options.E: A platelet count above 150 × 10⁹/L is required

explanation: Haemostasis in cirrhosis is rebalanced, with reduced procoagulant and anticoagulant factors. INR does not predict procedural bleeding, and FFP increases volume and portal pressure without benefit. Viscoelastic testing can guide targeted correction for high-risk procedures.
referenceText: EASL 2018 (decompensated cirrhosis) [64]; Wendon et al. 2017 (EASL acute liver failure) [234]

stem: After forceful vomiting, a patient develops severe chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema and a left pleural effusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Boerhaave syndrome is a full-thickness rupture of the distal oesophagus, usually left posterolateral, causing mediastinitis, pneumomediastinum and left pleural effusion. Diagnosis is by CT with oral contrast. Management includes broad-spectrum antibiotics and antifungals, nil by mouth, drainage and surgical or endoscopic repair.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: Why are antibiotics given to patients with cirrhosis presenting with GI bleeding?

options.B: They reduce infections, rebleeding and mortality
options.D: They prevent hepatic encephalopathy only, not infection

explanation: Bacterial infections occur in up to half of cirrhotic patients with GI bleeding and are associated with rebleeding and death. Short-term antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone 1 g/day in advanced cirrhosis or high quinolone resistance) reduces infections, rebleeding and mortality.
referenceText: de Franchis et al. 2022 (Baveno VII) [47]; EASL 2018 (decompensated cirrhosis) [64]

stem: Why is over-transfusion of red cells harmful in acute variceal bleeding?

options.B: It raises portal pressure, increasing rebleeding risk
options.E: It causes hypercoagulability and portal vein thrombosis

explanation: Volume expansion raises portal pressure and increases rebleeding risk. Baveno VII recommends a restrictive transfusion strategy with a threshold of 7 g/dL and target of 7–8 g/dL, adjusted for cardiovascular disease and ongoing bleeding.
referenceText: de Franchis et al. 2022 (Baveno VII) [47]; Villanueva et al. 2013 (transfusion in UGIB) [226]

stem: For non-paracetamol acute liver failure, which King's College criterion alone indicates transplant listing?
explanation: King's College criteria for non-paracetamol ALF: INR above 6.5, or any three of age below 10 or above 40, aetiology (non-A non-B hepatitis, halothane, drug idiosyncrasy), jaundice more than 7 days before encephalopathy, INR above 3.5 and bilirubin above 300 µmol/L.
referenceText: Wendon et al. 2017 (EASL acute liver failure) [234]

stem: A ventilated patient with severe pancreatitis has IAP of 23 mmHg and rising airway pressures but stable renal function. Which first-line medical measures are appropriate?

options.A: Prone positioning in all cases, with high PEEP to splint the abdominal wall
options.B: Optimise sedation, decompress with NG and rectal tubes, avoid positive balance, drain ascites
options.C: Increase IV fluid boluses to maintain abdominal perfusion pressure above 60
options.D: Raise the head of bed to 60°
options.E: High PEEP to splint the abdomen and counteract the raised pressure

explanation: WSACS recommends medical management of IAH: improving abdominal wall compliance (sedation, analgesia, neuromuscular blockade briefly), evacuating intraluminal contents, draining intra-abdominal fluid, avoiding excess fluids and optimising perfusion. Decompressive laparotomy is reserved for overt ACS refractory to these measures.
referenceText: Kirkpatrick et al. 2013 (WSACS abdominal compartment syndrome) [114]

stem: A patient on apixaban presents with life-threatening upper GI bleeding and haemodynamic instability. Which reversal approach is appropriate?

options.C: No reversal is possible, because apixaban has no reversal option available
options.D: Andexanet alfa or four-factor PCC, with resuscitation and endoscopy

explanation: For life-threatening bleeding on factor Xa inhibitors, the ACC pathway suggests andexanet alfa or 4F-PCC (if andexanet unavailable). Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran only; protamine reverses heparin; vitamin K reverses warfarin.
referenceText: Tomaselli et al. 2020 (ACC oral anticoagulant bleeding pathway) [214]; Laine et al. 2021 (ACG upper GI bleeding) [122]

stem: A patient with cirrhosis is somnolent but rousable, confused and disoriented to time and place, with asterixis. What is the West Haven grade?
explanation: West Haven grade 1 involves mild changes (short attention, euphoria); grade 2 lethargy, minimal disorientation and asterixis; grade 3 somnolence to semi-stupor, gross disorientation; grade 4 coma. Grade 3–4 patients may need airway protection.
referenceText: Vilstrup et al. 2014 (AASLD/EASL hepatic encephalopathy) [228]

stem: A cirrhotic patient meets criteria for HRS-AKI. What is first-line therapy?
explanation: Terlipressin with albumin (CONFIRM) improves HRS reversal; noradrenaline is an ICU alternative. Midodrine/octreotide is less effective. Strongest distractor: Midodrine/octreotide is inferior to terlipressin.
